presentingComplaint: Found drowsy at home beside empty medication blister packs
history: Brought to ED by family after being found unresponsive on her bed ~2 hours ago, next to empty packets of amitriptyline (from a relative's prescription) and an over-the-counter sedative antihistamine. Empty vodka bottle nearby. Known depression on follow-up with community mental health; a note was found. No prior overdose. Time of ingestion uncertain but likely within the last 2-4 hours. No seizures witnessed, no head injury, no fever, no infective symptoms.
examination: Drowsy, rousable to voice but not fully oriented (GCS 11, E3V3M5). Pupils dilated ~5 mm, sluggishly reactive. Dry warm flushed skin, dry mucous membranes, reduced bowel sounds, palpable bladder (urinary retention) — anticholinergic toxidrome. No focal neurological deficit, no neck stiffness, no rash. Chest clear, no aspiration signs at present. No injection marks, no organophosphate-type secretions.
imaging: CT head not indicated on initial assessment (no focal deficit, no trauma, toxidrome explains presentation); consider if fails to improve or focal signs emerge
finalDiagnosis: Acute drug intoxication / poisoning — tricyclic (amitriptyline) plus sedative antihistamine and alcohol co-ingestion with anticholinergic toxidrome
citations: AACT/EAPCCT Position Statements on Gastrointestinal Decontamination (activated charcoal) 2004; ACMT TCA toxicity guidance
contraindications: Avoid flumazenil empirically in mixed/TCA overdose — precipitates seizures and unmasks proconvulsant effect
Avoid Class Ia/Ic and Class III antiarrhythmics (worsen TCA cardiotoxicity); use IV sodium bicarbonate for QRS widening
Avoid physostigmine if TCA suspected — risk of asystole/seizure
edgeCases: TCA cardiotoxicity can evolve rapidly: watch for QRS >100 ms, terminal R wave in aVR, dysrhythmia and seizures even while sensorium looks stable
Delayed/staggered ingestion or co-ingested modified-release preparations can cause late deterioration despite initial mild picture
Anticholinergic toxidrome may mask/blunt expected bradycardia and mimic a hyperadrenergic state
expectedMaiK: This is an acute poisoning, not an infection — antibiotics are not indicated. Prioritise ABC, continuous cardiac monitoring and a 12-lead ECG looking for QRS prolongation and terminal R in aVR; give IV sodium bicarbonate if QRS >100 ms or ventricular dysrhythmia, and avoid flumazenil/physostigmine in suspected TCA co-ingestion.
expectedNextQuestions: Exactly what agents, how many tablets, and at what time were they taken (staggered vs single ingestion)?
Any co-ingestants including paracetamol, and access to modified-release formulations?
expectedInvestigations: 12-lead ECG (QRS duration, terminal R wave in aVR)
Paracetamol and salicylate levels, VBG, U&E, glucose

investigations: Capillary glucose and venous blood gas

regressionAssertions: expected.stewardship.tier must be null (non-infective — no antibiotic recommended)
